summary:
Rovers bound for the Moon's south pole are tested on Earth first. But at the pole the sun never climbs more than a few degrees. In our NASA SPICE calculation, it peaks at 1.56° on Shackleton's rim and 5.53° at Malapert Massif. No site in our catalog comes close to that light.

Earth Analog Explorer ranks 30 Earth sites against three targets: Shackleton rim and Malapert Massif on the Moon, and Jezero crater on Mars. It uses slope and roughness computed from NASA LOLA, SRTM and Mars 2020 elevation models. 18 of the 30 sites are new candidates that our scan found in 6,768 terrain windows.

Lighting is never blended into the score. It stands beside it, and the app warns when the terrain matches but the light doesn't. Seven of the ten best Malapert matches get that warning, including Mauna Kea, a NASA lunar field-test site.

Every value shows its source. Missing data stays "missing". A stability check reruns each ranking 1,000 times, and an AI assistant explains the results but cannot change a score.
details:
The problem: a perfect terrain match can still be the wrong light

Artemis will land near the lunar south pole. Malapert Massif has been on NASA's list of Artemis III candidate landing regions since 2022 (NASA 2022) and stayed on the narrowed list of nine in October 2024, and the ridges around Shackleton crater are among the most persistently lit ground on the Moon (Mazarico et al. 2011; Speyerer & Robinson 2013). The trade-off is that the sun stays on the horizon there. We computed the sun's position for every hour of 2026 from NASA NAIF SPICE ephemerides (DE440). It never rises above 1.56° at our Shackleton rim point or 5.53° at Malapert. On Earth the sun climbs high every day. Of the 30 Earth sites we rank, the site with the highest low-sun share is Haughton crater, at 36% of daylight hours. At both lunar targets the share is 100%.

That gap matters for rovers, because they see with cameras. NASA Ames built the POLAR stereo dataset to study this problem: rover-camera images of lunar-like terrain under polar lighting (Wong et al. 2017). The LuMon benchmark (Sekmen et al. 2026) shows a state-of-the-art depth model, Depth Anything V2, doing well on images from the Etna analog (δ1 = 1.00 and 0.88) and on Chang'e-3 lunar images (0.95), but scoring only 0.32 on CHERI, a dark low-light analog. LuMon also finds that crater and rock geometry hurts depth accuracy even more than shading does. So both the ground and the light matter, and a test site has to be judged on both. These published results are why we treat light as a first-class condition instead of a footnote; they motivate the design of the app. The app itself performs no image analysis and runs no depth model — it computes terrain descriptors and solar geometry.

ㅤ

What we built

Earth Analog Explorer is a public web app that ranks Earth sites as analogs for three targets: Shackleton rim and Malapert Massif on the Moon, and Jezero crater on Mars, where Perseverance drives.

1. Terrain Match (0 to 1): for every site and target we compute three standard terrain measures over a 6 km window on a 30 m grid: mean slope, 90th-percentile slope, and roughness at 150 m. This is the same family of slope and roughness measures used to map the Moon from LOLA (Rosenburg et al. 2011). The score is a weighted mean of how close each measure is to the target's.

2. Low-sun share: the share of daylight hours with the sun under 10°. For Earth sites we use pvlib, and for the Moon and Mars targets we use NASA NAIF SPICE kernels. As a cross-check, the SPICE method agrees with pvlib to within 0.0004 on three Earth sites.

3. Light-mismatch warning: for Moon targets, if Terrain Match is at least 0.80 but the low-sun share is under 0.25, the site is flagged: "the ground matches, the light doesn't". We never fold lighting into the score. That would hide exactly the disagreement a test planner needs to see.

4. New candidates: we did not just re-rank the usual list. Our scanner cut 40 DEM tiles into 8,686 windows and removed sea, water-like and duplicate windows, leaving 6,768. From those it kept up to 6 per target that are mostly bare ground in ESA WorldCover and at least 20 km apart, giving 18 candidates in total. The tiles we scanned are the areas around the known sites plus 11 regions we chose for arid, volcanic and polar terrain; they were not drawn from a published sampling scheme, so the candidates show what this method finds in those regions — not a survey of the whole planet.

5. Stability: each ranking is rerun 1,000 times with perturbed weights and inputs. The app reports how often each site stays in the top 3, so a judge can see which results are robust.

6. Explainable by design: every value carries its source and tier ("computed", "cited" or "missing"). The weight sliders re-rank live. An AI assistant answers questions about the current ranking, but it can only ask the deterministic engine to rerun; it cannot write a score.

7. What the terrain numbers can and cannot say. The three descriptors overlap: two of them summarise slope, so they are not three independent environmental axes. They measure landform shape, not material — no mineralogy, grain size or temperature enters the score. The low-sun share is likewise a single scalar fraction of daylight hours; it does not describe shadow length, contrast or permanently shadowed ground, which are what actually make polar light hard for a camera. It establishes that the light gap is real and large, not what a rover would see.

ㅤ

What we found

- Malapert: 10 of 30 sites have a Terrain Match of at least 0.80, and 7 of those 10 get the light-mismatch warning. One is Mauna Kea (Terrain Match 0.88, low sun 11%), where NASA and its partners ran lunar ISRU field tests in 2008 and 2010 (Sanders & Larson 2011). It is a good test site for ground and a poor one for polar light, and the app shows both at once. The best Malapert match is a new candidate from our scan in the Atacama near Yungay (0.92). It stays in the top 3 in 99.3% of the 1,000 reruns.

- Shackleton rim: 5 sites score at least 0.80, and 3 of them are flagged. The top match is a new candidate in the southern Altiplano (0.87, low sun 12%). The best unflagged high match is the McMurdo Dry Valleys in Antarctica (0.85, low sun 33%).

- Jezero (Mars): the top match is a new candidate in China's Qaidam Basin (0.99, top 3 in 97.4% of reruns). Geologists have proposed the Qaidam Basin as a Mars analog for its cold, dry, high-UV setting and Mars-like landforms (Xiao et al. 2017). We chose that region for scanning because it is arid, so this is agreement with the literature, not an independent discovery. For Jezero, lighting is shown for reference only (12% low sun, sun up to 89.5°): Mars has a normal day, so the polar-light problem is a Moon problem.

- For all three targets, a scan candidate outranks every known analog. The best known site ranks 3rd, 3rd and 6th. Scanning finds terrain that hand-picked lists miss.

ㅤ

What we tested and dropped

Before building, we tested whether a single "vision difficulty" score could predict how a depth model would do. We used 490 images: NASA Ames POLAR terrains 1 and 11, plus Chang'e-3. Shadowed pixels did score worse than lit ones (δ1 0.94 vs 1.00 on POLAR and 0.73 vs 0.80 on Chang'e-3). But shadow fraction did not predict per-image error (Spearman +0.06, p = 0.35), and neither did image-embedding distance (−0.04, p = 0.50). A flat-ground fit matched or beat the model on mostly flat scenes. So we did not ship a made-up vision score. We show terrain, computed; lighting, computed; and published depth results, cited and labelled as such.

ㅤ

Limits we state openly

- Weights, ranges and thresholds are provisional defaults in one config file. The sliders and the stability check show how much each result depends on them.

- Lighting is geometric sun elevation only. It leaves out terrain shadowing, albedo, dust and Earth's sky light, which fills shadows that are black on the Moon.

- Scan candidates are terrain and land-cover matches only. Nobody has checked them on imagery or in the field. We scanned 11 chosen regions plus the areas around the known sites, not all of Earth.

ㅤ

Who it is for and what it changes

It is for field-test planners and rover-perception teams choosing where to take hardware on Earth. The tool turns "this site looks like the Moon" into an answer with two parts: how close the ground is, and how different the light is. A team can pick the best terrain match on purpose, then budget for lighting tests elsewhere (a lab like the Ames POLAR testbed, or a high-latitude site in winter), instead of finding the gap after the field season.

ㅤ

How we built it

- Pipeline: Python with uv, Rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, pvlib, SpiceyPy (NASA NAIF CSPICE), Matplotlib and the ESA WorldCover cloud tiles.

- App: React, TypeScript and Vite, with Three.js for the two linked 3D relief views, tested by 186 Vitest tests. One of those tests checks that the browser engine reproduces the Python scoring fixtures exactly.

- Hosting: GitHub Pages, plus a Vercel function for the assistant.

- Everything is open source: https://github.com/azrialahmad/earth-analog-explorer

- Every dataset used by the app is listed with its owner, link and licence in docs/REFERENCES.md.

All scores on this page are read from the live app on November 15th, 2026; the app is the reference for every number here.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA LDEM 85S 20 m polar DEM (lunar terrain for Shackleton rim and Malapert)
SRTM 1 arc-second global DEM (Earth terrain, 60°S to 60°N; tiles via the AWS Terrain Tiles mirror)
Mars 2020 TRN CTX DTM mosaic, USGS/NASA (Jezero terrain)
NASA JPL NAIF SPICE generic kernels: DE440, lunar orientation, PCK, LSK (sun elevation at the Moon and Mars targets)
NASA Ames POLAR Stereo Dataset (used in our depth-model study; not shown in the app)
projectRefs: Copernicus DEM GLO-30, ESA (Earth terrain above 60° latitude)
ESA WorldCover 10 m 2021 v200 (bare-ground share, scan filter)
Chang'e-3 depth benchmark data (via LuMon; used in our depth-model study)
DLR S3LI Etna dataset (cited via LuMon)
